newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan murder clues hark back to US 'Zodiac' killer.
newsitem.headline: Japan murder clues hark back to US 'Zodiac' killer.

text.p: The 500-member detective squad investigating the murder and decapitation of a schoolboy in the central Japan city of Kobe last month have found similarities between the case and an unsolved 1960s U.S. killing spree.

Notes attached to the severed head of 11-year-old Jun Hase, whose body and head were found in separate locations on May 27, resemble messages written by the "Zodiac" killer who carried out a wave of killings in California beginning in 1966, Japanese media reports quoted investigators as saying.

The Zodiac killer sent taunting notes to the police and media every time he struck, with a cross drawn inside a circle similar to the mark the Kobe killer put on a cryptic message attached to the dead boy's head, the reports said.
Police last week released details of the message, part of which read:
"Now the game begins. Try and stop me, you stupid cops. I can't help but enjoy killing. I feel nothing but pleasure to see a person die."
Investigators suspect the killer may have learned of the 1960s Zodiac case through a book on unsolved crimes published in Japan in 1995, the reports said.
Meanwhile, more conventional clues also have emerged in one of modern Japan's most macabre crimes, which Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto has pledged an all-out effort to solve.
Eyewitnesses spotted a man in his 30s near the place where the boy's head was found and at about the same hour that police estimate the head was dumped.
The victim's head was found at the foot of an iron gate of a junior high school near Hase's home in Kobe's seaside suburb of Suma on May 27.
Separate eyewitnesses have reported seeing a suspicious vehicle parked near the boy's home on May 24, when he was last seen by his family. He left saying he was going to his grandfather's home.

In March, two young schoolgirls were attacked by a knife-wielding man near the school where the head was found, and one 10-year-old died. Police said there was no evidence so far that the cases were linked.

Some criminologists speculated that the suspect could be a man in his 30s with a deep grudge against the education system, because he mentioned schools in the note and left the head in front of a school.

The killing has sent tremors across Japan and has caused new anguish to the residents of Kobe, many of whom have only recently rebuilt homes and lives shattered by the powerful earthquake which killed 6,000 people in January 1995.
